Bipolar Disorder: Rule Out a Cause, Time the Episode, Then Treat

Mania or hypomania, and what to start or stop?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Hospitalize when needed to prevent harm: mania is an emergency.

Then rule out a drug or medical cause:

  • Urine drug screen
  • TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) and free thyroxine
  • CBC (complete blood count) and basic metabolic panel

Then time the episode:

  • Manic episode 1 week or more, or any length if hospitalized
  • Hypomanic episode 4 days or more in a row
  • Cyclothymic disorder 2 years or more of swings below episode criteria

One manic episode makes bipolar I disorder; psychosis, marked impairment or hospitalization makes an episode manic, never hypomanic.

Treat: stop any antidepressant; start lithium, valproate or a second-generation antipsychotic.

Diagnosis
Manic episode criteria Mood – elevated, expansive or irritable mood plus more energy, most of the day, nearly every day · Duration – 1 week or more, or any length if hospitalization is necessary · Symptoms – 3 or more DIGFAST symptoms, 4 if the mood is only irritable · Severity – marked impairment, hospitalization to prevent harm, or psychotic features · Cause – not a substance or medical condition; an episode that outlasts an antidepressant still counts · Mixed features – 3 or more depressive symptoms on most days of the episode
DIGFAST
  • Distractibility – attention too easily drawn to irrelevant stimuli
  • Indiscretion – painful consequences: buying sprees, sexual behaviours, foolish business investments
  • Grandiosity – inflated self-esteem
  • Flight of ideas – thoughts are racing
  • Activity increased – goal-directed, or psychomotor agitation
  • Sleep decreased – feels rested after only 3 hours
  • Talkativeness – pressure to keep talking
Management and treatment
Management ladder: acute manic episode
TierInterventionEscalate when
First lineStop antidepressants; lithium, valproate or a second-generation antipsychotic, alone or an antipsychotic plus lithium or valproateNo better after 2 weeks at therapeutic doses, adherence and substances checked
Add on or switchAnother first-line agent, added or switchedNo improvement after 2 weeks at therapeutic doses
Severe or resistantElectroconvulsive therapyTop rung
By situation Severe agitation or psychosis – sedating second-generation antipsychotic, sometimes lorazepam; lithium takes 4 to 10 days · Could become pregnant – avoid valproate: teratogenic · After remission – continuous maintenance for years; lithium lowers suicide risk · Bipolar depression – suicide risk first; quetiapine, lithium, lamotrigine or lurasidone; no antidepressant alone
Practice
  1. 31-year-old woman with 5 days of sleeping 4 hours without fatigue, faster speech and three new work projects; coworkers notice the change, but she still meets deadlines; major depressive episode 2 years ago; no delusions; toxicology negative; TSH normal → Bipolar II disorder → 4 or more days of symptoms others notice, without marked impairment or psychosis, plus a past major depressive episode
  2. 27-year-old man brought in after walking into highway traffic, laughing; 3 days without sleep, savings spent on a sailboat, talks without pause; admitted for his own safety; no delusions; no earlier mood episodes; toxicology negative; TSH normal → Bipolar I disorder → hospitalization satisfies both the duration and the severity criteria, so 3 days is enough
  3. 29-year-old man with 9 days of 3-hour nights, rapid speech and new business plans; believes God chose him as a prophet to lead the nation; still works daily; major depressive episode 1 year ago; toxicology negative; TSH normal → Bipolar I disorder → psychotic features make the episode manic by definition, even while he keeps working
  4. 38-year-old woman with 10 days of 2-hour nights, racing thoughts, nonstop talk, irritability and $9,000 of online purchases; most days she cries, calls herself a terrible mother and thinks of death; past admission for elevated mood; HR 88/min → Bipolar I disorder, manic episode with mixed features → full manic criteria plus at least 3 depressive symptoms (depressed mood, guilt, thoughts of death)
  5. 26-year-old woman started sertraline 4 weeks ago for a first depressive episode; for 8 days she sleeps 3 hours, talks rapidly, quit her job to launch three businesses and says she is destined for fame; HR 92/min; pregnancy test negative → Stop sertraline and start quetiapine → a full manic episode on an antidepressant: stop the antidepressant and start a first-line agent
  6. 33-year-old man found on his apartment roof at night announcing that he can fly; 9 days of almost no sleep; he gave away his car and talks nonstop; refuses admission, saying he has never felt better; toxicology negative → Inpatient psychiatric admission → hospitalization is needed to prevent harm to himself; mania is an emergency
  7. 29-year-old man in the emergency department shouting threats and throwing chairs at staff; a week without sleep; believes he is a secret agent chosen to save the world; similar hospitalization 2 years ago; glucose 96 mg/dL → Sedating antipsychotic and lorazepam → severe manic psychosis compromising safety needs rapid behavioral control; lithium takes 4 to 10 days
  8. 41-year-old woman hospitalized with elevated mood, no sleep, grandiosity and pressured speech has taken lithium for 16 days, at therapeutic levels for 14, every dose confirmed; toxicology negative; she is no better → Add quetiapine to lithium → no improvement after 2 weeks at therapeutic doses with adherence and substance use checked: add on or switch
  9. 24-year-old woman admitted with 10 days of little sleep, grandiosity, pressured speech and reckless spending; no psychotic symptoms; sexually active with inconsistent condom use; pregnancy test negative; TSH normal; toxicology negative → Divalproex → valproate should not be used in a woman of childbearing potential (fetal malformations, impaired intellectual development)
  10. 35-year-old man admitted 4 months ago for a week of no sleep, grandiosity and pressured speech has had normal mood for 3 months on lithium at therapeutic levels; BP 120/78 mm Hg; he asks to stop it → Continue lithium long term → maintenance for all patients with bipolar I disorder, continuous rather than intermittent
  11. 30-year-old woman with 3 weeks of depressed mood, loss of interest, oversleeping, fatigue and poor concentration; 2 years ago she was hospitalized for 10 days of no sleep, grandiosity and heavy spending; no suicidal thoughts; HR 72/min → Sertraline monotherapy → antidepressant monotherapy is not used in bipolar I depression and risks a switch to mania; quetiapine, lithium, lamotrigine or lurasidone is first line
  12. 45-year-old man on lithium for 6 years after two admissions for grandiosity and no sleep has 2 weeks of depressed mood, insomnia, poor appetite, slowed movements and hopelessness; says his family would be better off without him; HR 76/min → Assess suicide risk → most suicide deaths in bipolar disorder occur in the depressive phase, so suicide risk comes first
  13. 36-year-old woman with 8 days of little sleep, restlessness, rapid speech and irritability; 4-kg weight loss over 6 weeks; always feels hot; HR 118/min; fine tremor of the outstretched hands; toxicology negative → Serum TSH and free thyroxine → weight loss, heat intolerance, tachycardia and tremor point to hyperthyroidism, a medical cause of these symptoms
How NBME framed it: question 1

24-year-old receptionist at an accounting firm brought in by police; she cursed at a rental car agent and grew “out of control” when no luxury sports car was available. Examination normal. She asks for the physician’s number, winks, promises “a good time” and tries a kiss. Agitated; feels “absolutely fantastic”; loud, rapid speech. Says she is obviously very rich and the agents will regret delaying her for a television interview. Urine toxicology negative.

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder): hyperactive and impulsive; but ADHD is chronic and in more than one setting, and this is acute.
  • Delusional disorder: a fixed grandiose belief; but it has no mania beside the delusion.
  • Histrionic personality disorder: the wink and the attempted kiss; but personality disorders are chronic and pervasive.
  • Schizophrenia: a grandiose delusion; but it sits inside a manic episode (NBME cites missing negative symptoms).

Down to two: bipolar disorder or histrionic personality disorder. Bipolar disorder: the seductiveness sits inside an acute episode of euphoric, irritable mood with rapid speech, overspending and grandiosity.

How NBME framed it: question 2

43-year-old man admitted with superficial frostbite of the toes; police found him 5 hours earlier walking barefoot in a snowstorm. Says he is a god who can melt snow and purify the heart. Knows the date and place. Asked to recall red, penny, train, he laughs: “color, coin, conveyance.” Rapid, incessant speech; paces with arms raised, both index fingers aimed upward. Normal vital signs and laboratory results.

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Brief psychotic disorder: an acute delusion; but his psychosis is secondary to mania.
  • Delirium, alcohol withdrawal: found wandering in the cold; but vital signs are normal and he is fully oriented.
  • Delusional disorder: a fixed delusion; but it has no mania beside it.
  • Malingering: an odd, dangerous act; but nobody walks into frostbite for gain, and he has none.
  • Schizoid personality disorder: an odd man; but he is playful and talkative, not detached.
  • Schizophrenia: the god delusion and the posture; but the delusion is part of mania (NBME cites missing negative symptoms).

Down to two: bipolar disorder, manic, or schizophrenia. Bipolar disorder, manic: the delusion rides on rapid, incessant speech and more activity, with normal vital signs and full orientation.

The Patient on Lithium: Which Complication, and What to Do: what does maintenance lithium do to the kidney and thyroid? Delirium: Tell It From Dementia and Psychosis, Then Find the Cause: are attention and orientation intact? Part I Thyroid Mimics & Discriminators: is a thyroid cause driving the energy and weight loss?
Transferable rule

Before naming a psychosis or a personality disorder, rule out a drug or thyroid cause, then ask whether the symptoms sit inside a discrete episode of elevated or irritable mood with DIGFAST symptoms; if they do, it is mania, and any antidepressant stops.
